title: Backend Fundamentals and APIs: The Server Behind the Screen

questions.question: Which HTTP method should create a new resource, such as submitting a new order?
questions.rationale: POST submits data to create a new resource and is NOT idempotent — repeating it creates another order. GET only reads, PUT replaces an existing resource, and HEAD fetches headers only.

questions.question: An API replies with status 404. This means:
options: The requested resource was not found
questions.rationale: 404 Not Found is a 4xx CLIENT-side status: the URL points at no existing resource. A crash is 5xx (500), lacking permission is 403, and malformed input is 400.

questions.question: In a REST API, the URL design `DELETE /api/books/42` follows the REST convention because:
options: URLs should contain verbs like delete
The URL names a resource and the HTTP method expresses the action
REST requires the word api in every URL
questions.rationale: REST uses nouns for resources in URLs and lets the HTTP method (GET/POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE) express the verb. Read aloud it is 'delete book 42' — predictable for tools, caches, and other developers.

questions.question: The Express middleware line `app.use(express.json())` exists to:
options: Parse incoming JSON request bodies into req.body
questions.rationale: Express does not parse bodies by default; without this middleware req.body is undefined for JSON POSTs. It reads the request stream and attaches the parsed object to req.body.

questions.question: Why must a payment button be protected against double-clicking?
options: POST is not idempotent — resubmitting creates a second payment
Browsers cannot send two requests at once
questions.rationale: POST lacks idempotency: each submission creates a new resource. Robust APIs add idempotency keys so retries (double clicks, flaky networks) are recognised server-side and applied only once.

questions.question: In the browser, `const res = await fetch(url)` pauses:
options: The entire page's event loop until the server answers
Only the async function — the page stays responsive
questions.rationale: fetch returns a promise; await suspends just that async function's continuation while the event loop keeps serving clicks and rendering. That asynchrony is what keeps SPAs responsive during network waits.

questions.question: A JWT-based authentication flow identifies the user by:
options: A server-side session table keyed by cookie ID
Verifying the signature of a signed token sent with each request
questions.rationale: The server signs the token (e.g. with HMAC); every request carries it in the Authorization header, and the server verifies the signature — no session lookup needed. This statelessness scales across many servers.

questions.question: Which status code family indicates SERVER-side failure?
questions.rationale: 5xx means the server is at fault: 500 Internal Server Error, 502 Bad Gateway, 503 Unavailable. 4xx faults the client's request, 2xx is success, and 3xx is redirection.

questions.question: CORS errors appear because:
options: Browsers block cross-origin requests unless the server opts in with CORS headers
The API uses the wrong status code
questions.rationale: The same-origin policy blocks web pages from reading responses of other origins unless the server sends Access-Control-Allow-Origin (and friends). It is a browser-side protection, not a server bug — the fix belongs on the serving API.

questions.question: Why must backend code validate inputs even though the frontend already checks them?
options: Because anyone can bypass the UI and call the API directly with a tool
Validation is only a server-side concept
questions.rationale: The UI is a convenience, not a boundary: curl and scripts hit your endpoints with arbitrary payloads. Server-side validation of types, lengths, and permissions is the only line that cannot be walked around.
